facts.claim: OpenAI’s reasoning guide (vendor documentation, checked November 2026): lower effort favours speed and fewer tokens, and the hidden reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens.
Snell et al. (2024): on questions a smaller model can already sometimes solve, extra thinking at answer time beat a model 14 times larger, for the same compute.
Lewis et al. (2020): a model’s own store of facts is hard to reach and update, and looking passages up let it answer fact questions better and more accurately.
Cobbe et al. (2021, OpenAI): a checker trained to judge worked maths answers, picking the best of many tries, clearly lifted scores on grade-school word problems.
Snell et al. (2024): on the hardest questions, extra thinking helped very little, and a bigger, longer-trained model was the better spend.
Snell et al. (2024): choosing the thinking strategy per question by its difficulty used about 4 times less compute than a fixed best-of-many for the same score.
Ong et al. (RouteLLM, 2024): a cheap sorter choosing a strong or a weak model per question cut costs by over 2 times in some tests, with no loss in answer quality.
